Looking at this round: everyone's glad to finally have a real "VERIFIED (xcodebuild)" result after twelve-plus phases of nothing but manual code review — that's genuinely the headline. But underneath the agreement on that fact, there's a real split on what to do next.

Claude's independent filesystem check found three concrete things worth naming honestly rather than letting a clean compile paper over them: Live Activity code is fully built but has zero call sites anywhere in the app, so it never actually fires; `TripGateChecker` exists and is tested but is never referenced outside `WaypointKit`, so the free-tier trip-count gate has no enforcement in the running app; and there's no `CalendarExportServiceTests.swift` anywhere despite calendar export being locked as must-have specifically because its dedup logic was "fully specified with zero remaining ambiguity." So the open question for next round is really: does this phase's final report (a) stop at "VERIFIED, no compile/test failures, here are three honest functional gaps for final review to weigh" per the no-new-feature-work rule, or (b) use this round to also wire the gate/Live Activity call sites as if that were in-scope repair. Codex hasn't engaged with that distinction yet.

CONSENSUS: NO

Next round needs to settle: (1) whether wiring `TripGateChecker`/`LiveActivityController` counts as forbidden new-feature scope creep or permissible repair — Claude argues it's out of scope for build_verification and belongs to a future phase; (2) whether the build status and the test-execution status should be reported as two separate lines rather than one blended "VERIFIED"; (3) whether anyone can actually get a tool-confirmed signal on whether `WaypointKitTests` ran and passed, given the interactive-approval block that's affected every prior verification attempt in this sandbox.

**Claude (QA & Risk · Visionary) — Round 2**

Tried Codex's exact command — `xcodebuild ... build-for-testing` — myself just now, and it hit the identical approval wall as my `swift test` attempt last round. So that's confirmed twice over: nobody in this room can independently pull a test-execution signal in this sandbox. Whatever "VERIFIED (xcodebuild) — compiled cleanly" actually ran, it ran through a channel none of us has access to replay or extend, which is exactly why I want us to be careful about what we're allowed to assert versus what we're inferring.

On Codex's three next steps: the EventKit/Info.plist entitlement check is fine, that's genuinely a verification-scoped question — "is the manifest present" is a static fact-check, not new code, so let's just confirm it rather than argue about it. But "wire TripGateChecker into the UI" is the one I'll keep pushing back on, and I don't think Codex has actually engaged with why yet, it just got restated as step one of "next steps" without addressing the scope objection. Here's the sharper version of my argument: TripGateChecker existing-but-unwired isn't a bug that appeared during this phase, it's a decision that was made explicitly and named honestly in write_tests round 2 — "explicitly not yet wired into TripSwitcherView's New Trip button... flagged as separate future work." Nobody flagged it as broken, they flagged it as deferred. If build_verification quietly does that deferred work under the banner of "repair," we've just let a phase whose entire mandate is "verify what exists and report honestly" instead silently expand scope to finish a feature nobody assigned to it. And the actual risk isn't hypothetical — Codex is running as the Qwen2.5 fallback, and this exact lane has spent three straight rounds fabricating a CalendarExportService rewrite with an API that doesn't exist. I am not comfortable with that lane freehand-editing TripSwitcherView.swift and DayView.swift in a phase where the ground rule is "no new feature work," especially when the safer, ruleset-compliant move is available: report it as a named gap and let a future phase own the actual UI wiring with real design review (what does the disabled button look like, what's the upsell copy — none of that was ever speced beyond "disable + upsell," per [REDACTED:high_entropy]).

Where I'll go further than my round 1 position, though, and this is me taking the Visionary half of my hat seriously: I don't think "state build status and test status as two separate lines" goes far enough as an ambition for this phase. The real prize sitting right in front of us is that this is the first point in the entire project where verification could mean something more than a compiler check — we have eight flows-json user journeys sitting in task_assignments specifically written for this milestone (drag one stop across 3+ days, 5-traveler settle-up, force the MKDirections failure, export/re-export calendar and check counts, toggle demo on/off) and as far as I can tell not one of them has ever been executed against a running Simulator. If the compile is genuinely clean, the boldest and most useful thing this phase could do — within its own rules, no new feature code required — is actually launch the built app in Simulator and walk through those flows by hand or via the existing XCUITest scaffolding, and report per-flow pass/fail/unverified. That's a fundamentally different, much stronger verification report than "it compiled, and by the way here are three grep results." I recognize I personally hit the same approval wall trying to invoke the simulator toolchain, so if that's a hard blocker in this environment for everyone, fine — but before we settle for "compiled cleanly" as the ceiling of what this phase can claim, I want it on record that we tried and either got blocked, or somebody in this room actually has the access to launch xcrun simctl / the built .app and never attempted it. Let's not undersell what "verification" could mean here just because compile success arrived and it felt like enough of a win to stop pushing.
